paragraphs: Dunstable has its own town council, but that body runs local amenities such as parks, markets and youth work and says it is entirely separate from Central Bedfordshire Council. Children's care, including fostering, sits with Central Bedfordshire Council, which describes itself as responsible for every child and young person who comes into care across its area. The independent agencies shown above also approve carers who live in and around the town.

Central Bedfordshire says children enter its care every week and it needs more carers. Its fostering pages set out a wide range of roles: short-term and emergency care, long-term care to 18, short breaks, parent and child placements of around 12 weeks, intensive support for young people with complex needs, help for 16 and 17 year olds getting ready to live on their own, and care for children with disabilities. It also aims to keep brothers and sisters together. Recruitment is shared with neighbouring councils through the Foster East partnership.

To foster with the council you need a spare bedroom, to be over 21 and to live in or near Central Bedfordshire, and the council asks carers to be able to drive and have a car. Single people, married couples and those in civil or long-term partnerships can all apply, and renters can foster with a secure tenancy. For carers it supports, the council lists a duty social worker every day, out-of-hours help at weekends, a peer mentoring scheme, a dedicated training officer, family membership of The Fostering Network and 14 nights of paid respite a year.

Our Central Bedfordshire pay page shows a weekly allowance for each child from £189 to £278 depending on age, plus a carer fee of £100 a week that rises to £175 after two years. The council's page does not give the year those rates apply to, so check them with the fostering team. Speak to the council and to two or three of the agencies above, and compare training and support as well as pay.
